newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK govt urged to bare truth behind ousted official.
newsitem.headline: HK govt urged to bare truth behind ousted official.

text.p: The Hong Kong government came under mounting pressure on Saturday from local media and lawmakers to bare the facts behind the sudden departure last year of a former immigration chief.

Lawrence Leung, testifying under oath to a Legislative Council panel of inquiry, said on Friday that he was forced out of his job, contradicting the government's earlier version that his sudden retirement was for personal reasons.

Leung, whose mysterious departure in July 1996 caused an instant uproar, was responsible for passports and immigration security, highly sensitive areas in the run-up to Hong Kong's transfer from Britain to China in mid-1997.
Terming the turn in events as Hong Kong's version of the "Watergate", newspapers in the colony demanded all the facts from Governor Chris Patten's adminstration.

"Compare what Mr Patten and others said in July with the story which emerged yesterday. It is simply not good enough for the administration to hide behind wordplay and bureaucratic procedures to leave the public in the dark," the South China Morning Post said in its editorial.
The Hongkong Standard, argued the government's credibility was now at stake. "In the interest of open government, we must have some honest answers," it said.

Independent Chinese-language daily Ming Pao said it was now difficult for the government to hide the truth behind Leung's retirement, adding civil servants' morale would be affected if the facts were not laid out.
Secretary for Civil Service Lam Woon-kwong, who spoke to reporters late on Friday, said Leung decided to retire.
Lam said Leung had been presented with a choice between retiring or waiting for Lam to make a case to Patten that his retirement would be desirable in the interest of the public.
Lam refused to say why the government had contemplated Leung's retirement and skirted questions on whether Patten had known of the matter beforehand.
Prominent politicians have also hit out at the government.
Pro-democracy legislator Emily Lau questioned the testimonies senior government officials had given before an inquiry panel into the affair.
"I just don't know who to believe anymore and mind you, all these people took their oaths...and it seems now that some people are trying to mislead Legco," she said.
Legislator Allen Lee, chairman of the Liberal Party accused the government on radio of being dishonest over the affair and said the administration had a serious case to answer.
Patten, speaking from London, insisted the administration had been telling the truth and said the government would have more to say in a few days, government radio reported.
